II22A-01.correct_answer: Male peepers called less often at the Calder ponds than at the Ellery ponds.
II22A-01.explanation: Bellweather says traffic noise discourages calling "because the din drowns out their calls," while Cardenas "suspects road salt instead." The passage says the Calder ponds "collect just as much runoff from that highway through a culvert, but a tall earthen berm keeps them as quiet as the Ashby ponds," and that the Ellery ponds "lie beside the highway's noisiest stretch but uphill of it, so no runoff reaches them." Bellweather's hypothesis therefore predicts less calling at the noisy Ellery ponds than at the quiet Calder ponds, while Cardenas's account predicts less calling at the salted Calder ponds. The finding that "Male peepers called less often at the Calder ponds than at the Ellery ponds" is the opposite of what Bellweather's hypothesis predicts and fits Cardenas's, so it most directly weakens her hypothesis. The finding that "Male peepers called less often at the Ellery ponds than at the Ashby ponds" compares a noisy pond group that gets no runoff with ponds that "lie far from any road," so only noise differs and the finding supports Bellweather. The finding that "Male peepers called less often at the Brenlow ponds than at the Calder ponds" compares two groups that collect the same runoff, one noisy and one quiet, so it also supports Bellweather. The finding that "Male peepers called less often at the Brenlow ponds than at the Ashby ponds" is predicted by both accounts, since the Brenlow ponds "sit beside a highway and collect its salty runoff" and so have both noise and salt, so it cannot weaken Bellweather's hypothesis.

II22A-02.correct_answer: Seedlings died at a higher rate in the Cassel plots than in the Fairlie plots.
II22A-02.explanation: Andrade says the fungi "attack only this species and build up in the soil beneath its adults," while Ebbert says the seedlings "are limited by shade." The Cassel plots "lie in sunny gaps" whose soil "still holds as much of the fungi as soil beneath living adults," and the Fairlie plots "lie in sunny gaps far from any adult of the species." Both are sunny, so Ebbert's account predicts no difference between them, but only the Cassel plots hold the fungi. The finding that "Seedlings died at a higher rate in the Cassel plots than in the Fairlie plots" is therefore predicted only by Andrade's hypothesis and most directly supports it. The finding that "Seedlings died at a higher rate in the Bexleigh plots than in the Fairlie plots" compares deep shade from "adults of other species," which the fungi do not build up beneath, with a sunny gap without fungi, so only shade differs and the finding supports Ebbert. The finding that "Seedlings died at a higher rate in the Ardel plots than in the Cassel plots" compares two settings with the same amount of fungi, one shaded and one sunny, so it also supports Ebbert. The finding that "Seedlings died at a higher rate in the Bexleigh plots than in the Cassel plots" shows more deaths in shade without fungi than in sun with fungi, which is what Ebbert's account predicts and the opposite of what Andrade's predicts.

II22A-03.correct_answer: Robins along the bypass began singing earlier than robins in the lit lanes did.
II22A-03.explanation: Fairweather says streetlamps trigger the early singing "because the lamps' glow mimics daybreak," while Danvers says the robins start early "to get their singing done before morning traffic noise drowns it out." The passage says the bypass "carries just as much traffic but has no lamps," while the old-quarter lanes "are closed to cars and stay quiet until late morning," with some of them "lit all night." Fairweather's hypothesis therefore predicts earlier singing in the lit lanes than along the dark bypass, and Danvers's predicts the reverse. The finding that "Robins along the bypass began singing earlier than robins in the lit lanes did" is the opposite of what Fairweather's hypothesis predicts and fits Danvers's, so it most directly weakens her hypothesis. The finding that "Robins in the lit lanes began singing earlier than robins in the unlit lanes did" compares lanes that are equally quiet and differ only in lighting, so it supports Fairweather. The finding that "Robins on the downtown streets began singing earlier than robins along the bypass did" compares roads with the same heavy traffic that differ only in lighting, so it also supports Fairweather. The finding that "Robins on the downtown streets began singing earlier than robins in the unlit lanes did" is predicted by both accounts, since the downtown streets "are lit all night and carry heavy traffic from early morning," so it cannot weaken Fairweather's hypothesis.

II22A-04.correct_answer: Strain R-07 doubled in 41 minutes at 30°C, in 49 minutes at 50°C, and in 55 minutes in salt.
II22A-04.explanation: Elford requires that a strain's doubling time at 50°C be "no more than 10 minutes longer than its doubling time at 30°C" and that its doubling time in 5% salt be "under 60 minutes." Strain R-07 slows by 8 minutes (41 to 49) and doubles in 55 minutes in salt, so "Strain R-07 doubled in 41 minutes at 30°C, in 49 minutes at 50°C, and in 55 minutes in salt" shows a strain meeting both conditions. All four choices read the table accurately. "Strain R-31 doubled in 46 minutes at 30°C, in 63 minutes at 50°C, and in 50 minutes in salt" meets the salt condition, but its doubling time rises by 17 minutes at 50°C, more than the 10 allowed. "Strain R-8 doubled in 44 minutes at 30°C, in 48 minutes at 50°C, and in 70 minutes in salt" meets the heat condition (a rise of only 4 minutes), but 70 minutes in salt is not under 60. "Strain R-119 doubled in 52 minutes at 30°C, in 58 minutes at 50°C, and in 90 minutes in salt" also meets the heat condition (a rise of 6 minutes) but fails the salt condition.

II22A-05.correct_answer: At Carrow Point, 35 of the 64 nests monitored hatched at least one chick.
II22A-05.explanation: Eckhart says a colony holds steady only if "more than half of its nests hatch at least one chick" and reports that one colony "cleared that mark." At Carrow Point, 35 of 64 nests hatched, and half of 64 is 32, so "At Carrow Point, 35 of the 64 nests monitored hatched at least one chick" shows a colony above half. All four choices read the table accurately. "At Brisco Spit, 54 of the 120 nests monitored hatched at least one chick" gives the largest number of hatched nests among the choices, but half of 120 is 60, so 54 falls short. "At Avelin Bar, 44 of the 90 nests monitored hatched at least one chick" comes close, but half of 90 is 45, so 44 is just under half. "At Fallow Strand, 15 of the 40 nests monitored hatched at least one chick" is well under half, since half of 40 is 20.

II22A-06.correct_answer: leaves at Carrick contained 6.4 mg of flavonoid per gram, compared with 6.0 mg at Bramley.
II22A-06.explanation: Corliss claims that one population had leaves "containing less flavonoid than those of a population growing lower on the mountain." The table places Carrick at 1,800 meters and Bramley higher, at 2,200 meters, so "leaves at Carrick contained 6.4 mg of flavonoid per gram, compared with 6.0 mg at Bramley" shows the higher Bramley population with less flavonoid than the lower Carrick population, the departure the claim describes. All four choices read the table accurately. "leaves at Elstow contained 7.3 mg of flavonoid per gram, compared with 6.0 mg at Bramley" compares Elstow (2,600 meters) with the lower Bramley site, so the higher site has more flavonoid, as the general pattern predicts. "leaves at Aldwick contained 5.6 mg of flavonoid per gram, compared with 4.8 mg at Fenmore" likewise shows the higher site (Aldwick, 1,400 meters, versus Fenmore, 1,000 meters) with more. "leaves at Bramley contained 6.0 mg of flavonoid per gram, compared with 5.6 mg at Aldwick" also fits the pattern, since Bramley (2,200 meters) is higher than Aldwick (1,400 meters) and has more flavonoid.

II22B-01.correct_answer: There were more rockfalls from the north-facing cliff in July than from the north-facing cliff in March.
II22B-01.explanation: Grieg attributes the rockfalls to freeze-thaw cycles, while Lund attributes them to heavy rain, which falls "from June through August, when temperatures stay well above freezing." The north-facing cliff "begins to thaw by day and refreeze by night only in March and April," so on that cliff March brings freeze-thaw cycles but no heavy rain, and July brings heavy rain but no freeze-thaw cycles. Grieg's hypothesis therefore predicts more rockfalls there in March, and Lund's predicts more in July. The finding "There were more rockfalls from the north-facing cliff in July than from the north-facing cliff in March." is the opposite of what Grieg's hypothesis predicts, so it weakens it. The finding "There were more rockfalls from the north-facing cliff in March than from the north-facing cliff in January." supports Grieg: the north-facing cliff "stays frozen solid" from December through February, so only March has freeze-thaw cycles, and neither month has heavy rain. The finding "There were more rockfalls from the south-facing cliff in January than from the north-facing cliff in January." also supports Grieg, because in January the south-facing cliff "thaws on most afternoons and refreezes at night" while the north-facing cliff stays frozen, and neither cliff receives heavy rain then. The finding "There were more rockfalls from the south-facing cliff in January than from the south-facing cliff in July." supports Grieg as well, since January brings freeze-thaw cycles to the south-facing cliff while July brings it heavy rain without them.

II22B-02.correct_answer: Silver in sealed wool-lined cases tarnished faster than silver in ventilated cotton-lined cases.
II22B-02.explanation: Kaarsberg blames gases from wool felt, and Hult blames "polluted city air." A sealed case "keeps city air out but also traps any gases released inside the case," while a ventilated case "lets city air in but also carries gases from the lining away." So Kaarsberg's hypothesis predicts the fastest tarnishing in sealed wool-lined cases, and Hult's predicts faster tarnishing in ventilated cases whatever their lining. The finding "Silver in sealed wool-lined cases tarnished faster than silver in ventilated cotton-lined cases." pits the two accounts against each other: the sealed wool-lined case has the trapped wool gases but no city air, and the ventilated cotton-lined case has city air but no lining gases, because cotton "releases no sulfur." Only Kaarsberg's hypothesis predicts this result. The finding "Silver in ventilated cotton-lined cases tarnished faster than silver in sealed cotton-lined cases." involves no wool at all and is what Hult's account predicts. The finding "Silver in ventilated wool-lined cases tarnished faster than silver in sealed wool-lined cases." is also what Hult's account predicts, and it runs against Kaarsberg's, since the sealed case should trap the wool's gases. The finding "Silver in sealed cotton-lined cases tarnished faster than silver in ventilated wool-lined cases." contradicts both accounts: the sealed cotton-lined case has neither city air nor a sulfur-releasing lining, so it does not support Kaarsberg's hypothesis.

II22B-03.correct_answer: Eruptions at the Iselund field in 2000–2003 were less frequent than eruptions at the Iselund field in 2005–2008.
II22B-03.explanation: Lark claims the plant, which began pumping "in 2004," made the geysers erupt less often. The plant "draws water from beneath the Iselund field," and both 2000–2003 and 2005–2008 fall in the years of normal rainfall "between and since" the droughts, so Holm's account predicts no difference between them. Lark's claim predicts fewer Iselund eruptions after pumping began. The finding "Eruptions at the Iselund field in 2000–2003 were less frequent than eruptions at the Iselund field in 2005–2008." shows the opposite, so it weakens Lark's claim. The finding "Eruptions at the Kalvnesby field in 2000–2003 were less frequent than eruptions at the Kalvnesby field in 2005–2008." has the same shape but concerns the Kalvnesby field, where "its pumping does not reach the water," so Lark's claim makes no prediction there and the finding does not bear on it. The finding "Eruptions at the Iselund field in 2005–2008 were less frequent than eruptions at the Kalvnesby field in 2005–2008." is what Lark's claim predicts: in the same normal-rainfall years, only the Iselund field was affected by pumping. The finding "Eruptions at the Iselund field in 2009–2012 were less frequent than eruptions at the Kalvnesby field in 2000–2003." is predicted by both accounts, since Iselund in 2009–2012 had both pumping and drought while Kalvnesby in 2000–2003 had neither, so it cannot weaken Lark's claim.

II22B-04.correct_answer: Hesk Lake's ice cover fell from 148 days in the 1980s to 121 days in the 2010s, while Garvik Lake's fell from 142 days to 123 days.
II22B-04.explanation: Lidtke found that "Hesk Lake lost more days of ice cover than the deepest lake did." The table shows that Garvik Lake, at 64 meters, is the deepest of the five. Hesk Lake lost 148 − 121 = 27 days, and Garvik Lake lost 142 − 123 = 19 days, so the choice ending "Garvik Lake's fell from 142 days to 123 days" supports the finding. All four choices read the table accurately, and each shows Hesk Lake losing more days than the other lake named. But Jarnholt Lake (41 meters, a loss of 15 days), Lunmar Lake (8 meters, 22 days), and Ivren Lake (23 meters, 24 days) are not the deepest lake, so the choices ending "Jarnholt Lake's fell from 133 days to 118 days," "Lunmar Lake's fell from 156 days to 134 days," and "Ivren Lake's fell from 152 days to 128 days" do not address the comparison the finding makes. Jarnholt Lake had the fewest ice-covered days in the 1980s, but that does not make it the deepest.

II22B-05.correct_answer: the water from the Ivarsby well contained 38 micrograms of arsenic per liter.
II22B-05.explanation: Gjerde claims that a well "drawing from young sediment" can exceed the limit "even when the well is more than 100 meters deep." The table shows that the Ivarsby well is 115 meters deep and draws from young sediment, so the fact that "the water from the Ivarsby well contained 38 micrograms of arsenic per liter." (above the limit of 10) supports the claim. All four choices read the table accurately, and all four wells exceed the limit, but only Ivarsby meets both of the claim's conditions. The Gavlin well draws from young sediment but is only 45 meters deep, so "the water from the Gavlin well contained 52 micrograms of arsenic per liter." does not show a deep well exceeding the limit. The Haldor well is 130 meters deep but draws from old sediment, so "the water from the Haldor well contained 27 micrograms of arsenic per liter." does not concern young sediment. The Lindstrup well is 85 meters deep and draws from old sediment, so "the water from the Lindstrup well contained 14 micrograms of arsenic per liter." meets neither condition.

II22B-06.correct_answer: the layer at Joskar is 22 centimeters thick, compared with 14 centimeters at Ilvikmoen.
II22B-06.explanation: Gaard argues that at some site the layer "is thicker than it is at a site closer to the vent." The table shows that Joskar is 51 kilometers from the vent and Ilvikmoen only 38 kilometers, so "the layer at Joskar is 22 centimeters thick, compared with 14 centimeters at Ilvikmoen." shows a farther site with a thicker layer, as the argument requires. All four choices read the table accurately, but the other three each compare a nearer site with a farther one and show the nearer site's layer as thicker, the general pattern Gaard says is "as expected." Hanstrup (25 kilometers) is closer than Joskar (51 kilometers), so "the layer at Hanstrup is 31 centimeters thick, compared with 22 centimeters at Joskar." follows the pattern even though it involves Joskar. Gorvel (12 kilometers) is closer than Ilvikmoen (38 kilometers), so "the layer at Gorvel is 46 centimeters thick, compared with 14 centimeters at Ilvikmoen." follows it too. Hanstrup (25 kilometers) is also closer than Kelvane (64 kilometers), so "the layer at Hanstrup is 31 centimeters thick, compared with 9 centimeters at Kelvane." shows only ordinary thinning.

II22C-01.correct_answer: Morning test scores rose more at Nolvaston schools than at Rossmere schools.
II22C-01.explanation: Moreau holds that "eating breakfast sharpens students' concentration," while Okafor holds that the programs work "by drawing students to school early." The two accounts come apart at the Nolvaston schools, which "serve breakfast in classrooms after the first bell, and tardiness there has not changed": students there eat breakfast but are not drawn in early. Rossmere schools "offer no morning program." The finding that "Morning test scores rose more at Nolvaston schools than at Rossmere schools." therefore shows a gain where students ate breakfast without arriving earlier, which only Moreau's account predicts. The finding that "Morning test scores rose more at Mendrick schools than at Rossmere schools." is predicted by both accounts, since Mendrick students both eat breakfast and, as "tardiness there has fallen" shows, arrive earlier, so it does not favor Moreau. The finding that "Morning test scores rose more at Mendrick schools than at Nolvaston schools." compares two groups whose students both eat breakfast but only one of which is drawn in early, so it is what Okafor's account predicts. The finding that "Morning test scores rose more at Pemberwick schools than at Rossmere schools." describes a gain at schools that "serve no food" but where "tardiness there has also fallen," which is also what Okafor's account predicts and tells against Moreau's.

II22C-02.correct_answer: Teenagers in Pruett used the rising intonation more often than teenagers in Nantle did.
II22C-02.explanation: Paredes credits "daily face-to-face contact with Rensford teenagers," while Quayle credits "a popular radio program." The passage says the station "could be received in the valley's eastern towns, but a ridge blocked its signal from the western towns," and that teenagers from Mossbury and Nantle "attended high school in Rensford" while those from Pruett and Ombry "attended schools in their own towns." Pruett teenagers could hear the program but had no daily contact; Nantle teenagers had daily contact but could not hear the program. Paredes's account therefore predicts more use in Nantle, so the finding that "Teenagers in Pruett used the rising intonation more often than teenagers in Nantle did." runs against her hypothesis and fits Quayle's. The finding that "Teenagers in Mossbury used the rising intonation more often than teenagers in Ombry did." is predicted by both accounts, because Mossbury had both the contact and the signal while Ombry had neither. The finding that "Teenagers in Nantle used the rising intonation more often than teenagers in Ombry did." compares two western towns that both lacked the signal and differed only in contact, so it supports Paredes. The finding that "Teenagers in Mossbury used the rising intonation more often than teenagers in Pruett did." compares two eastern towns that both received the signal and differed only in contact, so it also supports Paredes.

II22C-03.correct_answer: On the fourth floor, employees in window seats reported higher job satisfaction than employees in interior seats did.
II22C-03.explanation: Rourke credits daylight, while Orsini notes that "window seats go to senior employees, and senior employees tend to report higher satisfaction." The passage says seats "on the third and fourth floors, however, were assigned by lottery," and that on "the first and third floors" the windows "admit little daylight," while "windows on the other floors look out over open sky." On the fourth floor, then, window seats get daylight but not senior occupants, so the finding that "On the fourth floor, employees in window seats reported higher job satisfaction than employees in interior seats did." can be explained by daylight and not by seniority, which most directly supports Rourke. The finding that "On the first floor, employees in window seats reported higher job satisfaction than employees in interior seats did." describes a floor where seats follow seniority but windows "admit little daylight," which is what Orsini's account predicts and Rourke's does not. The finding that "On the second floor, employees in window seats reported higher job satisfaction than employees in interior seats did." describes a floor with both open-sky windows and seniority seating, so both accounts predict it and it cannot favor Rourke. The finding that "On the third floor, employees in window seats reported higher job satisfaction than employees in interior seats did." describes a floor with lottery seating and little daylight, where neither daylight nor seniority separates the two groups, so it gives no support to Rourke's hypothesis.

II22C-04.correct_answer: In Nuskirk, reported nighttime burglaries fell from 30 to 23 a year.
II22C-04.explanation: Pike's claim needs a neighborhood where "reported nighttime burglaries fell by more than one-fifth." In Nuskirk they fell by 7, from 30 to 23, and one-fifth of 30 is 6, so "In Nuskirk, reported nighttime burglaries fell from 30 to 23 a year." shows a fall of more than one-fifth (about 23%). All four choices read the table accurately. "In Orvel, reported nighttime burglaries fell from 60 to 49 a year." describes the largest fall in number, 11, but one-fifth of 60 is 12, so the fall is less than one-fifth (about 18%). "In Rookwell, reported nighttime burglaries fell from 45 to 37 a year." describes a fall of 8, less than one-fifth of 45, which is 9. "In Ploverly, reported nighttime burglaries fell from 35 to 29 a year." describes a fall of 6, less than one-fifth of 35, which is 7.

II22C-05.correct_answer: Medlow drew 1,350 shoppers in an average week to its 30 vendors.
II22C-05.explanation: Okonkwo's claim needs a market that meets two conditions: "fewer than half of the vendors accepted cards," and "more than 40 shoppers per vendor." The table shows that 40% of Medlow's vendors accepted cards, and 1,350 shoppers divided among 30 vendors is 45 per vendor, so "Medlow drew 1,350 shoppers in an average week to its 30 vendors." meets both. All four choices read the table accurately. "Nevin drew 1,150 shoppers in an average week to its 25 vendors." works out to 46 shoppers per vendor, but the table shows that 72% of Nevin's vendors accepted cards, more than half. "Rushmere drew 2,100 shoppers in an average week to its 50 vendors." works out to 42 shoppers per vendor, but 58% of Rushmere's vendors accepted cards, also more than half. "Ossiter drew 1,400 shoppers in an average week to its 40 vendors." describes a market where only 35% of vendors accepted cards, but 1,400 shoppers among 40 vendors is 35 per vendor, fewer than 40.

II22C-06.correct_answer: salt cost 72 pence a bushel in Pirrock, compared with 66 pence in Quist.
II22C-06.explanation: Mabry's claim needs "a town farther from Ravenhythe" that "paid less for salt than a town nearer to it." The table places Quist 70 miles from the port and Pirrock 57 miles away, so "salt cost 72 pence a bushel in Pirrock, compared with 66 pence in Quist." shows the farther town, Quist, paying less than the nearer one. All four choices read the table accurately. "salt cost 58 pence a bushel in Orrowick, compared with 72 pence in Pirrock." compares Orrowick (41 miles) with Pirrock (57 miles), and the nearer town paid less, which fits the general pattern. "salt cost 52 pence a bushel in Nolsby, compared with 58 pence in Orrowick." compares Nolsby (28 miles) with Orrowick (41 miles), where again the nearer town paid less. "salt cost 66 pence a bushel in Quist, compared with 52 pence in Nolsby." compares Quist (70 miles) with Nolsby (28 miles), and the farther town paid more, as distance alone would predict.

II22D-01.correct_answer: Windmills replaced watermills more often in the Wrennick villages than in the Skarra villages.
II22D-01.explanation: Thorvald argues that "a drying climate drove the change," because "streams fed only by rain ran too low to turn a waterwheel." Sorensen argues that villagers built windmills "to avoid the fees that lords charged for grinding grain at a manor's watermill." The Wrennick and Skarra villages both "owed no manor fees," so Sorensen's account gives neither group a reason to switch and predicts no difference between them; the two groups differ only in that the Wrennick villages "stood on rain-fed streams" while the Skarra villages stood on spring-fed streams, "which flow steadily all year." The finding that "Windmills replaced watermills more often in the Wrennick villages than in the Skarra villages" is therefore predicted only by Thorvald's account, so it most directly supports her hypothesis. The finding that "Windmills replaced watermills more often in the Udsen villages than in the Skarra villages" compares two groups on spring-fed streams that differ only in whether they owed manor fees, which is what Sorensen's account predicts, not Thorvald's. The finding that "Windmills replaced watermills more often in the Thrane villages than in the Skarra villages" compares villages that differ in both fees and streams, so both accounts predict it and it cannot favor Thorvald. The finding that "Windmills replaced watermills more often in the Udsen villages than in the Wrennick villages" favors villages that owed fees but had steady streams over villages that owed no fees but had rain-fed streams, the opposite of what Thorvald's account predicts.

II22D-02.correct_answer: Pipes in organs built by the Ulving workshop were more corroded than pipes in organs built by the Tamm workshop.
II22D-02.explanation: Wennberg blames "acetic acid vapor given off by the oak cases," while Yderberg blames damp, noting that the stone churches "stay humid for much of the year" and the timber churches "stay dry." Ulving organs have pine cases, which give off "far less acetic acid," and stand in stone churches; Tamm organs have oak cases and stand in timber churches. Wennberg's hypothesis therefore predicts more corrosion in Tamm organs than in Ulving organs. The finding that "Pipes in organs built by the Ulving workshop were more corroded than pipes in organs built by the Tamm workshop" shows the opposite: the organs with less acid but more damp corroded more, which fits Yderberg's account and most directly weakens Wennberg's. The finding that "Pipes in organs built by the Selander workshop were more corroded than pipes in organs built by the Ulving workshop" compares organs in the same kind of church that differ only in case wood, so it supports Wennberg. The finding that "Pipes in organs built by the Tamm workshop were more corroded than pipes in organs built by the Vass workshop" makes the same comparison for timber churches, so it also supports Wennberg. The finding that "Pipes in organs built by the Selander workshop were more corroded than pipes in organs built by the Vass workshop" compares oak cases in damp churches with pine cases in dry ones, so both accounts predict it and it cannot weaken Wennberg's hypothesis.

II22D-03.correct_answer: Houses built in Tolvik in the 1740s had larger windows than houses built in Saltrup in the 1740s.
II22D-03.explanation: Varga credits cheaper glass from the Svarte glassworks, which opened "in 1735" and whose glass "was shipped only by barge to towns on the Tessel River." Tamsen credits a fashion spread by pattern books "that circulated throughout the valley from about 1720." Tolvik stands "on the river," while Saltrup lies "in the hills, far from any navigable water." By the 1740s both towns had the pattern books, but only Tolvik could get the cheap glass, so Tamsen's account predicts similar windows in the two towns and Varga's predicts larger windows in Tolvik. The finding that "Houses built in Tolvik in the 1740s had larger windows than houses built in Saltrup in the 1740s" therefore most directly supports Varga's claim. The finding that "Houses built in Saltrup in the 1720s had larger windows than houses built in Saltrup in the 1710s" shows windows growing in a hill town after the pattern books arrived but before the glassworks opened, which is what Tamsen's account predicts, not Varga's. The finding that "Houses built in Wennor in the 1740s had larger windows than houses built in Yvenby in the 1710s" compares a river town that had both the pattern books and the glass with a hill town that had neither, so both accounts predict it. The finding that "Houses built in Yvenby in the 1740s had larger windows than houses built in Tolvik in the 1720s" compares two cases that both had the pattern books and neither had the cheap glass (Yvenby is a hill town, and those Tolvik houses predate 1735), so it gives Varga's claim no support.

II22D-04.correct_answer: at Tarrow Mill, the engine burned 96 kilograms of coal per hour before the refit and 60 kilograms after it.
II22D-04.explanation: Stenholm points to "a mill whose refitted engine burned less than two-thirds as much coal per hour of work as it had before." At Tarrow Mill the engine burned 96 kilograms before the refit and 60 after; two-thirds of 96 is 64, and 60 is less than 64, so "at Tarrow Mill, the engine burned 96 kilograms of coal per hour before the refit and 60 kilograms after it." completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. Two-thirds of Wedda Mill's 60 kilograms is 40, and its engine still burned 42, so the Wedda choice fails even though it shows the smallest amount burned after a refit. Two-thirds of Sorrel Mill's 75 kilograms is 50, and its engine still burned 53. Two-thirds of Yarrel Mill's 150 kilograms is 100, and its engine still burned 105, so the Yarrel choice fails even though it shows the largest drop in kilograms (45).

II22D-05.correct_answer: printed books averaged 6.0 grams of silver per 100 leaves in the 1500s and 5.1 grams in the 1510s.
II22D-05.explanation: Tovesen notes "a case in which book prices fell from one decade to the next even though the price of paper held steady." From the 1500s to the 1510s, paper stayed at 19 grams of silver per ream while printed books fell from 6.0 to 5.1 grams per 100 leaves, so "printed books averaged 6.0 grams of silver per 100 leaves in the 1500s and 5.1 grams in the 1510s." completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. The choices covering the 1470s to the 1480s (9.6 and 7.8 grams) and the 1510s to the 1520s (5.1 and 4.0 grams) show book prices falling, but over both of those steps paper also fell, from 31 to 25 grams and from 19 to 15 grams, so cheaper paper could account for them. The choice covering the 1480s to the 1490s is the one other step in which paper held steady, at 25 grams, but book prices rose from 7.8 to 7.9 grams rather than falling.

II22D-06.correct_answer: Sollen Hall has a reverberation time of 1.45 seconds, 640 seats, and a volume of 5,440 cubic meters.
II22D-06.explanation: Yttergren's two conditions are a reverberation time that "falls between 1.4 and 1.7 seconds" and "at least 8 cubic meters of volume for each seat." Sollen Hall's reverberation time of 1.45 seconds is in that range, and 5,440 cubic meters divided by 640 seats is 8.5 cubic meters per seat, so "Sollen Hall has a reverberation time of 1.45 seconds, 640 seats, and a volume of 5,440 cubic meters." completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. Teverin Hall's 1.60 seconds is in range, but 6,150 cubic meters for 820 seats is only 7.5 cubic meters per seat. Wrayne Hall's 1.55 seconds is in range, but 3,375 cubic meters for 450 seats is also only 7.5 per seat, even though it is the smallest hall. Ulmar Hall provides 10 cubic meters per seat (5,600 for 560 seats), but its reverberation time of 1.90 seconds is above the range.
